doc.title: Lou Marini interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 15, 2023

title: Synthesizers, computers and lost work
summary: Joe Wilder on staff work disappearing, earlier technological job losses, and Marini's views on electronic versus human music.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: I’m just reading a book — I got to know Joe Wilder.
Oh man, I loved him man.

Oh, what a — I mean who couldn’t love Joe Wilder? Musically and personality-wise. And he described exactly what you were just saying, that there was so much work, he was on staff and he played the television orchestras. And then, even back then, he talked about “and then the synthesizer came in” and so I guess some things never change.

Yeah. Well you know it’s not the first time that musicians got out of work. When talking movies took over, overnight basically, within a year or so or a couple of years, thousands and thousands of gigs from guys playing in movie theaters just disappeared. So you know I listened — like I was listening to the soundtrack last night of a series, a contemporary Swedish series that I’m watching on Netflix. And I realized that these computer sounds, they’re just a part of our lives now you know. The atmospheric sounds in certain kinds of scenes in these series and movies that we go to have been subsumed by these sounds that can only be made by synthesizers. So I’m sure that there is going to be great music that’s going to come out of these sounds but I don’t think it’s happened yet you know. And there’s also something about, you know when I listen to these vocoder vocals, and the drum and especially the rhythm tracks, you know you could just as easily be listening to a washing machine. When you consider like Luis Conte is always playing, because he’s such a master percussionist. He’s always playing stuff for us from like African tribal music or Caribbean or Brazilian or — and you listen to this stuff and it’s so much more complex. And the grooves are so intense that it makes the electronic stuff seem stupid. It seems infantile compared to what humans do on the nach. And I think about like what young people are listening to and it’s like this mechanical stuff that has no soul to it, and if even the vocal is manipulated then even the vocal sound is not like hearing the richness of a singer like Ella Fitzgerald or Jack Jones or Red Prysock. I mean you know it’s just — you wonder where it’s going you know. © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-
